passages.t: Be ready: the brothers are sent ahead
passages.happening:
Paul says he hardly needs to write about the gift (verse 1). He knows the Corinthians are eager. He has even boasted about them to the Macedonians: “since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise” (verse 2).

But he is sending the brothers ahead, so that his boasting will not prove empty (verse 3). He is honest about why. If Macedonians come with him and find nothing ready, both he and the Corinthians will be ashamed (verse 4).

So the brothers will help them make the arrangements beforehand. “This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its main city. Paul uses the eagerness of each region to stir the other. He told the Corinthians about Macedonia (8:1-5), and the Macedonians about Corinth. It is a gentle kind of friendly competition.

Shame and honour mattered greatly in that world. To make a public promise and not keep it brought disgrace. Paul does not want that for the Corinthians, and he admits he does not want it for himself either.

The word translated ‘generous gift’ in verse 5 is eulogia. Word for word it means ‘a good word’, ‘a blessing’. A gift freely given is a blessing to the one who receives it. The opposite, says Paul, is a gift squeezed out of someone, given ‘begrudgingly’. The Greek word there is linked to greed: holding on tight and letting go only under pressure.

Paul plans ahead so that no one is pressed at the last minute. A gift gathered slowly and freely is better than one demanded in a rush when the visitors are at the door.
passages.ot:
Paul's careful planning has a model in Israel's history. When the people brought gifts to build the tabernacle, they brought so much that Moses had to tell them to stop: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary” (Exodus 36:6).

Keeping a promise made to God is an old teaching. “When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Yet the same book adds, “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). Paul wants the Corinthians' promise to become a gift, not a burden or an embarrassment.
passages.asks: Paul planned ahead so that the giving would be free and not rushed. Ask whether there is a promise you have made, to God or to someone else, that is still waiting. Ask how you could keep it gladly, not under pressure at the last moment.

passages.t: Sowing and reaping: ‘God loves a cheerful giver’
passages.happening:
Paul gives a picture from the farm. “Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously” (verse 6).

The gift must be free. “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (verse 7).

God will supply them. “And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work” (verse 8). Paul quotes a psalm: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever” (verse 9).

God gives the seed and the bread. He will “increase the harvest of your righteousness” (verse 10). “You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, so that through us your giving will produce thanksgiving to God” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Everyone in Corinth knew farming. A farmer who keeps his seed in the barn for fear of losing it will have a poor harvest. One who scatters it freely will have more. Paul uses this common wisdom about generosity.

‘Cheerful’ is the Greek hilaros. It is where the English word ‘hilarious’ comes from, but it does not mean funny. It means glad, from the heart. It comes only here in the New Testament. ‘Compulsion’ means pressure from outside. Paul does not want gifts pulled out of people by guilt, fear or a public appeal they could not refuse.

Look at the word ‘all’ in verse 8. In Greek it comes again and again: all grace, all things, all times, all that you need, every good work. God is not stingy.

But read carefully what God gives and why. He gives ‘all that you need’, so that they can do ‘every good work’. The harvest is ‘the harvest of your righteousness’. They are ‘enriched in every way to be generous’. And the end of it all is ‘thanksgiving to God’. The return on giving is more giving, and more praise of God. Paul does not say the giver will become wealthy.

Paul's own life shows this. He was often hungry and poor (11:27). He called himself “poor, yet making many rich” (6:10). And the Macedonians he praised gave out of ‘deep poverty’ (8:2).
passages.ot:
Proverbs taught the same wisdom. “One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor” (Proverbs 11:24). “A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor” (Proverbs 22:9).

‘God loves a cheerful giver’ is not found in the Hebrew of Proverbs or in the BSB's Old Testament. But the old Greek translation of Proverbs adds a line after 22:8 about God blessing, or loving, a cheerful and generous man. Paul's words are close to that line.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9: “He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Psalm 112:9). In the psalm the giver is “the man who fears the LORD” (Psalm 112:1). The BSB prints ‘His’ with a capital in 2 Corinthians, reading it as God. Readers differ. Either way the point holds: God gives freely, and those who fear him become givers like him.

Verse 10 echoes Isaiah, where God's word is like rain, “providing seed to sow and food to eat” (Isaiah 55:10). ‘The harvest of your righteousness’ may echo Hosea: “Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion” (Hosea 10:12).
passages.hard:
Does ‘whoever sows generously will also reap generously’ mean that giving money to God will make you rich?

No. These notes say so plainly. Some teachers say that if you give to God, or to their ministry, God will pay you back with more money, sometimes many times over. This is often called prosperity teaching, or the prosperity gospel. It is one of the things this site does not teach as true. Many who teach it are sincere, and many who believe it are hoping for help in hard times. But it is a mistake, and this passage does not support it.

Here is why. Paul says God will give ‘all that you need’, not all that you want. The harvest he names is ‘the harvest of your righteousness’: goodness, not goods. The riches are ‘to be generous on every occasion’, so that people thank God. And the people in these chapters who give most freely are poor and stay poor. To turn giving into a way of getting more makes it a deal with God. That is the opposite of grace. Jesus warned, “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

God does care for those who give. Many Christians can tell of times when he met their needs. That is true, and it is a reason for trust. It is not a formula.

Is a tenth, a tithe, the rule for Christian giving? This passage does not say. It speaks of what each one ‘has decided in his heart’. The note on Genesis 14:17-20 sets out how Christians answer the tithe question, and the Honest Answer ‘What does the Bible actually say about money?’ says more.

If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says God loves a cheerful giver, not a pressured one. Ask what you give, and how you feel when you give it. Then ask what your giving is for. Is it to get something back, or because God has already given to you, so that others may thank him?

passages.t: ‘Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift’
passages.happening:
Paul lifts his eyes from Corinth to Jerusalem. The gift will do more than meet needs. “For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints, but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God” (verse 12).

The believers in Jerusalem will see the proof of the Corinthians' faith. They will “glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all the others” (verse 13).

They will pray for the Corinthians and long for them, “because of the surpassing grace God has given you” (verse 14).

And Paul ends the two chapters in worship. “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘This ministry of service’ uses the Greek word leitourgia. In Greek cities it was a public service that a rich citizen paid for, such as a festival or a ship. In the old Greek translation of the Old Testament it was used for the work of priests in worship. The English word ‘liturgy’ comes from it. So the gift is both a service to others and an act of worship.

In a patron's world, those who received a gift owed the giver honour. Paul turns that around. The poor in Jerusalem will not owe the Corinthians anything. Their answer will be thanks to God and prayer for the givers. The honour goes to God, the first giver.

The gift also joins two kinds of believer. Jewish Christians in Jerusalem and Gentile Christians in Greece had mostly never met. Some on each side may have doubted the other. A gift and the prayers it brings back would knit them together.

‘Indescribable’ is anekdiēgētos, ‘beyond telling’. It comes only here in the New Testament. Most readers take God's indescribable gift to be Christ himself, whom Paul named in 8:9. After two chapters about giving, Paul admits that God's own gift cannot be put into words.
passages.ot:
Gifts that turn into praise are an Old Testament pattern. When the people gave freely for the temple, “the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders, for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly” (1 Chronicles 29:9). Then David praised God before the whole gathering.

The psalms call for thanks to God for his unspeakable goodness. “Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise?” (Psalm 106:2).

And the prophets pictured the nations bringing gifts to Jerusalem: “the wealth of the nations will come to you” (Isaiah 60:5). Some readers think Paul saw the Gentile churches' gift as a small sign of that hope. Paul does not say so here, but the picture of Gentiles giving to Jerusalem fits it.
passages.asks: Paul ends with thanks to God, not with praise for the givers. Ask what you would put on a list of God's gifts to you. Then ask whose thanks to God your giving might bring about, and whom you might pray for as the Jerusalem believers prayed for Corinth.
